Skin tones in a text column, with their denominator

Source: R/emoji-identity.R
emoji_skin_tone.Rd

emoji_skin_tone() counts, per row, the emoji that can carry a skin tone, how many of them do, and which tones they carry. It describes the glyphs a text uses and never infers anyone's skin colour or identity; see Glyphs, not people in tidyEmoji.

Usage

emoji_skin_tone(data, text, presentation = "emoji")

Arguments

data

A data frame or tibble containing a text column. Grouped data frames are accepted. The verbs that work a row at a time (adding columns, or keeping and expanding rows) carry the grouping through to their result, as dplyr::mutate() and dplyr::filter() do. The verbs that pool across rows – the counts, the co-occurrence edge lists, the time series – warn that they ignore the grouping and return one corpus-wide answer.

text

The text column to scan, supplied unquoted. Any atomic column is accepted and read as character, so a factor works and a numeric, Date or logical one simply contains no emoji. A list column – or a data-frame column – is refused rather than coerced, because coercing one deparses it and the emoji found would be in the code rather than in your data. What counts as an emoji is the same in every verb; see the Detection section of tidyEmoji for the one case that surprises people, code points that are emoji only when they carry U+FE0F.

presentation

Which code points count as emoji: "emoji" (the default) or "any".

  • "emoji" requires emoji presentation, so U+2764 U+FE0F is an emoji and the bare U+2764 is not. This is the default and it will stay the default: widening it would silently recount every corpus already analysed.

  • "any" also reads the text-presentation spellings Unicode lists for an emoji (the bare heart, U+263A, U+2714, a keycap without its selector), because several keyboards emit them. It never reads the copyright, registered and trade-mark signs (U+00A9, U+00AE, U+2122), which are typography far more often than they are emoji.

"any" only ever adds occurrences: everything "emoji" finds, it finds too, in the same place. emoji_coverage() reports how many it adds and how many of those a lexicon can score, which is the cost of the choice in one number. Every verb that counts, scores or rewrites the emoji in a text column takes this argument, so counts still agree across the package for whichever value you use. The flag verbs do not need it, since a flag has no text-presentation form.

Value

data, as a tibble, with added columns .emoji_n_modifiable (occurrences of an emoji that can take a tone, toned or not), .emoji_n_modified (those that carry one), .emoji_n_light, .emoji_n_medium_light, .emoji_n_medium, .emoji_n_medium_dark and .emoji_n_dark (tone instances, so a couple in two tones adds to two columns and one in a single tone adds two to one), .emoji_n_mixed (occurrences carrying two or more distinct tones), .emoji_n_orphan_modifiers (swatches standing alone) and .emoji_tone (the row's one tone, "default", "mixed" when its tone-able emoji differ, or NA when it has none). A grouped input stays grouped.

Details

Both halves of that sentence have evidence behind them. Writers mostly choose a tone close to their own (Robertson, Magdy and Goldwater 2018, 2020), so tones are informative about writers in aggregate; and readers infer the writer's identity from a tone, the default yellow included (CSCW 2021), which is exactly why a tool must not. "default" means a tone-able emoji written without a tone, which is a keyboard setting on some platforms and an active choice on others.

Report the denominator. The share of tone-able emoji that carry a tone differs tenfold between corpora: 88.9% of 117 on the tweet sample this package bundled until 0.7.0, 9.2% of 782 in all of OASST2, 8.0% of 1,445 in a WildChat shard, and 23.2% of 181 in oasst_messages, whose half carrying emoji was sampled for them. A bare percentage cannot tell a difference in the writers from a difference in which emoji they chose, so the verb returns the two counts and leaves the ratio to you, which is also what makes it right for any grouping:

emoji_skin_tone(d, text) |>
  dplyr::group_by(author) |>
  dplyr::summarise(modified = sum(.emoji_n_modified),
                   modifiable = sum(.emoji_n_modifiable),
                   share = modified / modifiable)

A swatch standing alone, as in U+1F600 U+1F3FB, where the face cannot take the tone, is no emoji (see the Detection section of tidyEmoji) and so in none of the tone counts; .emoji_n_orphan_modifiers accounts for it.

References

Robertson, A., Magdy, W. and Goldwater, S. (2018). Self-representation on Twitter using emoji skin color modifiers. ICWSM 2018, 680-683.

Robertson, A., Magdy, W. and Goldwater, S. (2020). Emoji skin tone modifiers: analyzing variation in usage on social media. ACM Transactions on Social Computing 3(2). doi:10.1145/3377479

Black or white but never neutral: how readers perceive identity from yellow or skin-toned emoji (2021). Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction 5 (CSCW2). doi:10.1145/3476091

See also

emoji_decompose() for one glyph at a time; emoji_retone() to rewrite the tones for an experiment.

Examples

d <- data.frame(text = c("thanks \U0001f44d\U0001f3fd",
                         "\U0001f44d and \U0001f44b\U0001f3ff",
                         "a \U0001f600\U0001f3fb b"))
emoji_skin_tone(d, text)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 11
#>   text      .emoji_n_modifiable .emoji_n_modified .emoji_n_light
#>   <chr>                   <int>             <int>          <int>
#> 1 thanks 👍🏽                   1                 1              0
#> 2 👍 and 👋🏿                   2                 1              0
#> 3 a 😀🏻 b                      0                 0              0
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: .emoji_n_medium_light <int>, .emoji_n_medium <int>,
#> #   .emoji_n_medium_dark <int>, .emoji_n_dark <int>, .emoji_n_mixed <int>,
#> #   .emoji_n_orphan_modifiers <int>, .emoji_tone <chr>
